title: How Antidepressants Work
summary: Josh and Chuck (with the iHeart intro voice) tackle antidepressants as a tangential episode, since the show has never done a core episode on depression. They cover the overview of major depressive disorder, the biological (serotonin imbalance) model and its challenges, and newer theories about neuroplasticity. The episode walks through drug classes: SSRIs (fluoxetine/Prozac, paroxetine/Paxil, sertraline/Zoloft, fluvoxamine/Luvox, escitalopram/Lexapro, citalopram/Celexa), tricyclics from the 1950s and 60s, SNRIs (duloxetine/Cymbalta, venlafaxine/Effexor), NaSSAs, and MAOIs (discovered by accident while testing TB drugs, marsilid, tyramine and the cheese reaction). It then covers supplements like St. John's wort and their lack of regulation, psychedelics (ketamine/esketamine approval in 2019, psilocybin studies including a Johns Hopkins study), treatment phases (acute, continuation, maintenance), debate over prescription increases, and reasons antidepressants can worsen mood. The episode closes with a listener mail about hypnagogic imagery.

entities.name: University of Colorado study on neuroplasticity

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: The hosts joke about editing out Jerry and introduce the episode as a tangential one, since they have never done a core episode on depression.

segments.title: Depression overview and prevalence
segments.summary: Josh and the co-host discuss depression's prevalence, the difference between major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder, World Health Organization projections, and symptoms such as sadness, disrupted sleep, and loss of pleasure.

segments.title: History of depression treatment and the film Melancholia
segments.summary: The hosts describe historical treatments such as melancholy, black bile theory, and early remedies, stress that depression is highly treatable, and mention Melancholia as an accurate portrayal of depression.

segments.title: Biological model and how antidepressants act
segments.summary: The hosts explain the biological model that attributes depression to serotonin imbalance, note studies showing people with MDD do not have lower serotonin, and describe antidepressants as interfering with neurotransmitter reuptake at the synapse.

segments.title: Neuroplasticity theory of depression
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a University of Colorado study proposing that depression involves stuck brain circuits and that antidepressants may help repair neuroplasticity, supported by psychedelic treatments.

segments.title: Serotonin's other functions and side effects
segments.summary: Serotonin regulates sleep, digestion, nausea, clotting and bone growth, so altering it can cause side effects. The hosts make a table-setting joke before a break.

segments.title: SSRIs: names and mechanism
segments.summary: The hosts introduce SSRIs as the most frequently prescribed modern antidepressants, first available in 1988 with fluoxetine. They list generic and brand names and explain that SSRIs block serotonin reuptake so more stays in the synapse.

segments.title: SSRI effectiveness, advocacy, exercise and dosing
segments.summary: SSRIs are described as the flagship antidepressant with fewer side effects, and some patients need to try different ones. The hosts stress patient advocacy and exercise, mention Gary Greenberg's social media posts, and describe fluoxetine's long half-life and low starting doses to reduce side effects.

segments.title: Tricyclic antidepressants
segments.summary: Tricyclics from the 1950s and 60s were early antidepressants that block reuptake of multiple neurotransmitters non-selectively, causing more side effects and overdose risk. They are now used for neuropathic pain. An FDA black box warning about suicidality is discussed.

segments.title: SNRIs and NaSSAs
segments.summary: SNRIs block reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, starting in the mid-1990s, with duloxetine (Cymbalta) and venlafaxine (Effexor) named, and they perform about as well as SSRIs. NaSSAs, a related class from the mid-1980s, have different side effects such as weight gain and sedation.

segments.title: MAOIs and the cheese reaction
segments.summary: MAOIs inhibit monoamine oxidase, which breaks down tyramine, so dietary tyramine in foods like aged cheese can cause dangerous blood pressure spikes. MAOIs were discovered by accident while testing TB drugs in the early 1950s; marsilid, from 1958, was the first MAOI antidepressant, but they are rarely prescribed now.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before moving to nutraceuticals.

segments.title: Nutraceuticals and supplements for depression
segments.summary: Supplements are described as unregulated in the US, leading to concerns about dose consistency and purity, and studies of them give mixed results and can have side effects.

segments.title: St. John's wort
segments.summary: St. John's wort was popular in the 1980s and has long been used for mood, but it reduces the effectiveness of birth control pills and pharmaceutical antidepressants and affects antihistamines.

segments.title: Ketamine and esketamine
segments.summary: Ketamine was developed in the 1960s in Belgium and has been studied as a breakthrough treatment. The FDA approved esketamine in 2019 for treatment-resistant depression, and it is considered a last resort.

segments.title: Psilocybin studies
segments.summary: Psilocybin is described as effective for depression, with a Johns Hopkins study from 2022 showing large symptom reductions lasting up to a year after two doses, and a 2024 study suggesting it is at least as effective as SSRIs.

segments.title: Treatment phases: acute, continuation, maintenance
segments.summary: Treatment is described in phases: acute treatment, where antidepressants are tried for weeks to months; continuation after remission, lasting about six months; and maintenance, where relapse is possible and the prior drug may be restarted.

segments.title: Are antidepressants overprescribed and use in kids
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether antidepressants are overprescribed, noting that longer prescriptions inflate numbers and that tricyclics are used for pain. They cite a 66 percent rise in monthly prescriptions for ages 12 to 25 from 2016 to 2022, and discuss FDA approval ages, with the youngest found being seven.

segments.title: Why antidepressants can make depression worse
segments.summary: Possible reasons include misdiagnosis such as bipolar disorder or borderline personality disorder, genetics such as the SLC6A4 serotonin transporter gene, slow drug metabolism, being under 25, akathisia, and polypharmacy.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: The hosts encourage listeners with depression to seek treatment and say things can get better.

segments.title: Listener mail on hypnagogic imagery
segments.summary: A listener named Jill from Connecticut writes about the hypnagogic stage before falling asleep, when thoughts become strange or hallucinatory, and asks whether Chuck's experience is verbal or visual.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The iHeart sign-off closes the episode.
